newsitem.title: USA: May budget figures show deficit steadily shrinking.
newsitem.headline: May budget figures show deficit steadily shrinking.

text.p: A steadily expanding economy helped shrink the government's spending deficit by 8.6 percent to $48.5 billlion in May from $53.1 billion a year earlier, the Treasury Deparetment said on Friday.

The year-over-year improvement was even more dramatic for the first eight months of fiscal 1997, which ends on Sept. 30, as the cumulative deficit plummeted 40 percent to $65.4 billion from $108.4 billion in the comparable fiscal 1996 period.

"If present trends continue, the budget deficit could balance itself within two years, even without resolution of the ongoing budget wrangling," said economist Michael Fenollosa of John Hancock Financial Services in Boston.
Congress and the White House currently are arguing over tax changes needed to implement a budget-balancing agreement reached last month that called for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years.

The Treasury report showed that last month's deficit followed a $93.94 billion surplus in April, when revenues were boosted by payments from individuals complying with the mid-month filing deadline for 1996 tax returns.
Total government spending in May was $142.99 billion, up from $134.65 billion in April but down from $143.17 billion spent in May 1996.
Revenues from taxes, fees and other sources dropped to $94.49 billion in May from $228.59 billion in April. A year earlier, in May 1996, the government took in $90.12 billion in revenues.

During May, receipts from individual tax payments -- the biggest single source of government income -- dropped back to $30.7 billion from $134.3 billion in April. Corporate tax payments declined to $4.3 billion in May from $27.4 billion in April.

The improvement in the monthly deficit during May and for the first eight months of the year would have been even greater except that military active pay, veterans' benefits and supplemental security income payments scheduled for June 1 were moved up to May 30.
The payments were made early because June 1 fell on a weekend and waiting until after that time to mail out government checks would have meant delays for recipients.
The Clinton administration has officially forecast a deficit for all of fiscal 1997 of $125.59 billion, compared with a $107.4 billion shortfall in fiscal 1996.
But swelling government receipts appear certain to bring the deficit well under the White House estimate, which is expected to be revised when it issues its mid-year economic review later this year.

Private-sector analysts say the fiscal 1997 deficit will come in well under $100 billion, which would mark a fifth straight year of improvement since the government's spending deficit peaked at $290.4 billion in fiscal 1992.
John Hancock's Fenollosa said he estimated the fiscal 1997 deficit will be $67 billion.

He added that there was a possibility it could be slightly lower if economic growth exceeds expectations or if a tax pact includes large enough cuts in taxes levied against capital gains from stock investments to spur selling aimed at taking profits from the robust stock market, which would put more taxable income in consumers' pockets.
